fullText:
US cybersecurity researchers who conducted hack say ‘scope of what we could theoretically access was huge’

Cybersecurity researchers have hacked into OpenAI with the help of Anthropic’s Claude chatbot, in the latest example of security issues at the company.

A team at a US-based startup compromised a number of OpenAI employees’ ChatGPT accounts, starting a process that enabled them to access their target’s software cache – and potentially more.

“The scope of what we could theoretically access was huge,” said researchers at Hacktron AI.

Initially, the research team used Claude, which can generate code for hackers, to access ChatGPT accounts via an OpenAI staff discussion forum hosted by the Discourse platform. They then made a harmless “pull request” – an attempt to change the code in a file – to OpenAI’s service on the GitHub software repository.

Hacktron reported the hack to OpenAI, having carried out the operation under an OpenAI programme that rewarded ethical hackers for testing its systems. The researchers stressed that they had access to, but did not download, the code from the GitHub repository.

Despite initial use of Claude, the researchers said they were largely using OpenAI’s own cutting edge GPT-5.6 Sol model to carry out the hack, which was first reported by the Wall Street Journal.

An OpenAI spokesperson said: “We thank the researchers for contacting us and sharing their findings”, adding that the company had addressed the vulnerabilities that had been exploited.

Hacktron said AI tools had made a once-complex hacking task far easier and drastically shortened the time needed to plan and execute an attack. This is a common refrain from cybersecurity experts when discussing the impact of AI.

“Work that once required a well-resourced team and months of effort can now be compressed into days,” said Hacktron, which received a $6,500 payment from OpenAI under the company’s bug bounty programme.

The hack is the latest safety incident at OpenAI, which revealed in July that a “swarm” of agents – the term for AI tools capable of carrying out tasks autonomously – powered by its technology had hacked the AI startup Hugging Face during a cybersecurity test.

This week the San Francisco-based company revealed six more examples of “unexpected or concerning” actions by its technology, and warned that the pace of development could not continue at “maximum speed for much longer”.

Anthropic made a fresh call at the weekend for a slowdown in AI development, which was supported by OpenAI, Google DeepMind and Elon Musk. Anthropic also repeated warnings that unrestrained AI development posed an existential threat, concerns that some experts are sceptical about.

Donald Trump has rejected calls for a slowdown, citing a need to stay ahead of China’s AI industry and dismissing “negative forces … bringing up things that won’t happen”.

AI Is a Kitchen-Table Issue
description: Chris...
fullText:
And with the Trump administration encouraging unregulated growth in the industry, Democrats need to start acting like it.

The Republican Party sports a glaring weakness in the pitched battle over regulating the rapidly multiplying abuses of AI, and its name is Donald John Trump. The president sought to dismiss the growing furor about the multitude of threats the unregulated new technology poses to our basic quality of life by proclaiming on Truth Social that “the only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!”

But while the MAGAfied GOP is ambling cluelessly into yet another political firestorm, the Democratic Party is lapsing once more into its resting-shrug posture. Yes, there are serious hazards associated with the blind lunge into all things AI—up to and including species extinction—party elders and strategists concede, but it’s important not to get carried away on the tide of public outrage. So, as Trump fulminated and flattered himself, House minority leader Hakeem Jeffries announced the appointment of a new AI policy panel made up mostly of flacks and shills for the industry. Because whenever the leaders of an economic sector let it slip that they may well be programming the imminent demise of humanity, the first thing you do is grant them the authority to make up their own rules of oversight.

Jeffries’s gambit was, alas, a continuation of the party’s dilatory-to-negligent approach to all things AI. During the 119th Congress, Democratic lawmakers have mostly marshaled themselves behind vague and airy bids to draft regulation of the industry through bipartisan task forces stressing broad alignment on the issue, an approach that has yielded much the same results the most such initiatives do. “Congressional leaders have let bipartisan working groups fall apart, dragging out progress on issues lawmakers from both parties say they could get a meaningful majority behind,” NOTUS reporter Samuel Larreal wrote late last year. Even though some 400 pending bills in 2025 had addressed the many threats poised by untrammeled AI development, none gained traction; indeed, the most dogged GOP-driven campaign was to deregulate the industry further, via language in both the tax-and-spending and defense authorization bills that would have preempted state and local governments from curbing the growth of AI data centers and applications in their midst.

This lost opportunity stands out in high relief now, as Democratic leaders try to launch belated new bids to rein in the excesses of the AI sector before Congress adjourns for the midterms—and as a new cohort of Democratic-aligned PACs push for a more robust Democratic response to the uprising against it. (Lest you think this latter development signals any sort of fundamental change in establishment thinking, the party’s lead consultants and strategists are still urging candidates to avoid angering AI moguls in the homestretch of the midterms, lest they unleash their well-funded PACs on rebellious Democratic candidates in tight races.) The specter of yet more legislative hand-waving in the face of a mounting oligarchic assault on the basic quality of life in thousands of American communities is especially hard to take, the industry’s predations fall into the category that Democrats continually insist is the topic of their laser-focused attention: the frantic, unsupervised buildout of AI capacity is the essence of a kitchen-table issue.

Leaving aside the speculative forecasts of the technology’s potential role in snuffing out humanity, AI is already acting as a fearsome accelerant on the growth of inequality in the United States. It’s not hard to see why: The AI investment bubble, which has been set aloft on a series of circular financing schemes benefiting the tech power elite, has created an upward surge in the distribution of wealth that makes the run-up to the 2008 Great Recession look like the Paris Commune. JPMorgan estimates that just 30 AI stocks have added $5.2 trillion in paper wealth to US households—with most of that return confined to the top 10 percent of investors. Indeed, the bubble has accounted for an additional $180 billion in spending from these rarefied households, the Morgan analysts found, as most middle- and working-class households fend off higher energy and healthcare costs while sinking ever deeper into debt. While reports claim that AI investment now accounts for 40 percent or more of the country’s GDP growth, the subset of economic actors actually benefiting from the bubble is vanishingly small—and are mostly confined to the charmed circle of the tech oligarchy. Fully 80 percent of the enterprise revenues claimed by Anthropic and OpenAI, writes industry critic Ed Zitron, “are dependent on what are likely hundreds of customers spending outsized amounts of money on AI tokens, with an indeterminately-large chunk of them being AI startups that can only do so as long as venture capital supports them.”

And just like the mid-aughts housing bubble, the AI investment stampede is creating acute conditions of inequality on the ground—in towns, school districts, and workplaces. To begin with, there’s the push to cram data centers into virtually any low-tax, underregulated jurisdiction that can be cajoled into housing them. These engines of water scarcity, electricity-bill spikes, and noise pollution are the prime mover behind the populist uprising against AI in red and blue states alike, with hapless elected officials and candidates awkwardly vying to keep up. Polling shows that 75 percent of Americans oppose the erection of data centers in their communities, with just 15 percent supporting them.

The runaway appropriation of resources, land, and capital by the AI sector is, in other words, the mother of all kitchen-table issues—and by extension, shopfloor, roadway, and classroom ones, as our data lords seek to annex virtually every facet of our productive and civic life into their feverishly privating hands. Public education, long held to be the magic elixir of upward social mobility in the US economy, is rapidly becoming a bot playground, with predictably harmful fallout for students’ cognitive development while fomenting an epidemic of cheating and fraud. While early forecasts of an AI job apocalypse appear overblown, the technology’s role in promulgating surveillance-state protocols on the job decidedly is not.

So why is it that Democrats remain on their back heels in the midst of the AI uprising? One key explanation is that they benefit from the same Big Tech donations that have juiced Republican campaign coffers. Hakeem Jeffries has opposed a moratorium on data-center construction, and has detailed industry mouthpieces like California Representative Zoe Lofgren to draw up the Democratic caucus’s AI policy. This disconnect between the party’s leadership caste and the specter of a grassroots revolt in an election cycle has become so pronounced that former president Barack Obama has intervened. “This is something that is moving very fast in private hands, and if we don’t get on top of it, I think can be dangerous,” Obama told Jeffries at a New York City donors’ event last week. Looking ahead to the 2028 presidential cycle, he cautioned that Democratic candidates must have a “very clear plan” to address the imminent risks posed by the technology. “I would talk about this, and I would say, ‘Here’s our plan for safety. Here’s our plan for making sure our kids are not corrupted by this.’”

Obama, a longtime confrere of Big Tech titans, explained that he regards himself as neither a “doomer” or “accelerationist” on the AI front—but his political advice recalls the same lurch into populist rhetoric that attended his 2012 reelection campaign, when he had the great good fortune of drawing private capital baron Mitt Romney as his opposing candidate. As was the case then, Democrats have a terminally out-of-touch apostle of the investment class symbolizing the rush to adopt AI at all costs: President Donald Trump, who has fruitlessly sought to tamp down the rebellion against data centers in the house of MAGA. At the outset of his second term, Trump issued an executive order dismantling the Biden White House’s body of safety protocols governing the industry, while his Environmental Protection Agency and Justice Department have dedicated themselves to speeding along the unregulated rollout of data centers.

Trump is also, as a majority of polled respondents now acknowledge, staggeringly corrupt, so it shouldn’t be a heavy lift for Democrats to make the case that his desperate shilling for data centers—like his self-interested reversal on crypto and a fetid run of stock trades outpacing the investment calls of every member of Congress during his second term—serves to line his pockets and shower more pelf on his inner circle of cronies. Just for starters, Donald Trump Jr.’s venture-capital fund 1789 Capital has realized returns of more than 200 percent as of the end of this June, with many of the gains coming from aggressive AI investments.

The attack ads pretty much write themselves: Donald Trump is despoiling your communities, spiking your utility bills, rationing your water, and leaving your kids at the mercy of robots so he can clean up even more on the AI bubble. All we need now is a political party with the backbone to make them credible.

Between the reemergence of right-wing red-baiting and Donald Trump’s use of the chilling National Security Presidential Memorandum–7 to criminalize left political organizing, we’re seeing McCarthyism reborn before our eyes. 

This assault on democracy cannot be ignored or wished away. Resisting it requires bravery in the face of threats and repression, a steadfast commitment to the truth, and the unwavering belief that we can—and will—overcome this darkness.

We must have an independent media that sets the record straight, unearths corruption and abuses of power, and advances a politics of justice and dignity for all if we’re to win this fight.

That’s why I’m writing to you today. This September, The Nation needs to add 100 monthly donors to sustain our progressive journalism. Your contribution makes the next investigative report, the next truth-speaking column, and the next pathbreaking essay all possible. 

I hope you’ll support our work with a recurring donation today. If you donate $10 or more a month, we’ll send you a brand new “Hands Off the Free Press!” sticker to recognise your commitment to our cause. Please, donate today.

Onward,

Katrina vanden Heuvel
Editor and Publisher, The Nation

title: Proton partners with Apertus, Switzerland's sovereign AI model
description: Proton has partnered with the team behind Apertus, adding their sovereign AI model to its privacy-first AI chatbot Lumo.
fullText:
Proton is partnering with the team behind Apertus to bring its new Apertus 1.5 model to Lumo, Proton’s privacy-focused alternative to ChatGPT. The partnership will also give researchers behind Apertus access to real-world feedback that can help them improve it more quickly.

Apertus is a fully open large language model developed by researchers at EPFL(new window), ETH Zurich(new window), and the Swiss National Supercomputing Centre (CSCS). Its architecture, training data, and methods are open, and it’s trained on publicly available data, respecting opt-out requests and filtering out personal details. It fills an important role in today’s AI landscape by providing a fully open source model with a transparent and reproducible training pipeline. In a world dominated by US and Chinese models, Apertus is instrumental in Europe’s tech sovereignty.

The world’s leading AI models have millions of people using them every day, creating real-world feedback loops that help make them better. Fully open models developed in an academic context do not have access to feedback at the same scale, limiting their ability to compete at the frontier.

With this partnership, that could start to change. Proton is introducing a feedback mechanism that connects people using Apertus in Lumo with the researchers building it. Tens of millions of Lumo users around the world can now choose to contribute feedback, helping independent, ethical, and truly open source AI become more competitive.

Europe now has the pieces of an independent AI stack: infrastructure it controls, a model open by design, and a product that puts it directly in people’s hands.

“We don’t want to spend the next decade relying on other countries for the AI we use every day,” said Eamonn Maguire, Director of AI at Proton. “Having our own AI isn’t enough. It needs to be competitive so that people actually use it. This partnership with the Swiss AI Initiative gives Europe a path to get there.”

One of the biggest advantages leading AI labs have is a constant stream of feedback from millions of people using their models. Bringing Apertus to Lumo gives the university research teams behind it access to this feedback at scale, helping level the playing field.

To start using Apertus in Lumo, select Apertus 1.5 from the model dropdown, and start chatting as normal. Like other conversations in Lumo, your chats are protected by zero-access encryption and stay private by default.

If you choose to give feedback on an Apertus response, tap the thumbs-up or thumbs-down button to send in your feedback. Your contribution will be anonymized, and made available to the university research teams behind Apertus.

“Real-world feedback is the one ingredient that open models have been missing. Thanks to Proton, Lumo users will be able to voluntarily provide feedback that contributes to Apertus research. For a fully open, publicly developed model, that is a game changer,” says Imanol Schlag, Research Scientist at the ETH AI Center and co-lead of the Apertus project.

“Making Apertus available in Lumo gives us valuable insights into how the model performs in real-world settings. Voluntary feedback also helps us identify where it can be made more useful and more robust,” says Martin Jaggi, Professor at EPFL and co-lead of the Apertus project. “It also means that we are enabling a broader community to contribute to the model’s further improvement.”

Building an open and independent AI ecosystem is bigger than any one model or company. To compete in AI, Europe needs to pool its resources and build public-private partnerships that can do what no single organization can achieve alone. Europe’s future in AI depends on researchers building in the open, infrastructure governed in Europe, companies turning that technology into products people can use, and people willing to help those technologies improve.

Through this partnership, we are taking steps to make that alternative more than an idea. Starting today, fully open source AI is now something people can use and — if and when they choose to — help shape for the future.

title: Bring Your Own Agent
description: Stop putting an AI assistant in every product. Give the agent you already use access to your tools and data.
fullText:
Twenty years after getting rid of Clippy, we appear to have decided that we need 100 clippies rather than one.

Every product is getting a little intelligence-shaped thing in
the sidebar that wants to summarize, suggest, explain and occasionally do something on your behalf.
Jira has Rovo.
Sentry has Seer.
Salesforce had Einstein (but I guess that name was a bit too much – it’s gone now).

I get it: nobody wants to become the next Kodak.
CEOs love telling investors they’re still relevant.
And there might even be an occasional user actually aksing for this stuff.

But personally, I would rather have one agent that can use all my tools than a separate one living in each.

So if yet another agent isn’t the solution, what is?
I’d say: just give me my data!
Make sure you have a great API, or maybe even slap an MCP on top of it.

This way, the agent that I was using anyway can just reach inside and do its thing.
No need to have 5 imaginary friends passing notes to each other if I can bring my tool of choice.

You’re reading this post on the blog of Bugsink: a tool to keep Track of Errors in your (production) applications.
I happen to believe that Error Tracking is actually a pretty sweet fit for the “agentic age”:
Error Trackers are built to collect meaningful context, and Agents are built to consume it.

That doesn’t mean I’m about to force my own particular agent on you though: first, it’s simply not what I’m about (see the above) and
second, I don’t believe competing directly with the billions of the big AI labs is such a good game to be in in the first place.

Putting the AI in the product may still have its uses, of course: when a company can do analysis across millions of
its customers’ data sets, it may learn things that each individual customer (or their agent) wouldn’t be able to figure out.

The obvious problem with that setup is that it requires each of those customers to give up their data.
That’s problematic to begin with, but if the data contains the customers’ customers’ data (as it often does in the case of Error Trackers) the problems become even more serious.

I suspect we’ll look back at this phase as we now do on the time everybody and their dog wanted to tack their own social media platform onto their website (remember, kids?)

For now, I think the best thing we can do is to make sure our tools are actually useful to the agents our users
choose to use.

title: Microsoft exec called AI scraping 'the largest theft of labor in human history'
description: Newly unsealed court filings show Microsoft privately called OpenAI's data practices "theft" while both companies scraped paywalled Times content, built datasets from it, and warned internally it would gut publishers.
fullText:
New unredacted information in the copyright lawsuit The New York Times brought against OpenAI and Microsoft three years ago reveals an admission that AI scraping was tantamount to theft, and that AI products pose a major threat to publications.

Per the lawsuit, a top Microsoft executive privately described the companies’ AI training practices as “theft,” and OpenAI’s own leadership said its AI models posed an “existential threat” to the publishers and journalists whose work trained them.

The unsealed material also details how the companies allegedly obtained and used that content by bypassing paywalls undetected, building training datasets via mass scraping, and deliberately stripping copyright notices from training data.

It’s worth noting that much of the new information comes from The Times’ own brief, not the underlying exhibits, which remain sealed. The quotes below are presented without their original context.

The unredacted filing is the latest escalation in the three-year-old lawsuit, in which The New York Times initially alleged the firms violated copyright law by training generative AI models on its content.

The question of whether AI firms can legally use copyrighted material to train AI has no clear answer, but judges have been largely favorable to AI companies’ arguments that training constitutes “fair use.” This legal rule lets people use copyrighted work without permission in certain cases, like parody, news reporting, or criticism. Earlier this month, the Trump administration contributed a brief in defense of OpenAI’s unlicensed use of copyrighted material to train its LLMs.

Several of the new admissions, however, run counter to OpenAI’s fair use defense, particularly the rule’s requirement that use doesn’t substitute or harm the market for the original work.

For example, Microsoft’s own data shows its Copilot “answer engine” caused click-through rates for The New York Times’ domain to drop as much as 93% compared to traditional Bing search. An internal Microsoft presentation written by Microsoft’s director of Applied Science, Brent Hecht, in January 2024 describes the decline as a “doom loop” that would “hurt the performance of our models and the entire web at the same time.”

“It is highly unusual that an end-product threatens the economic foundations of its essential suppliers, but that is the situation we have created for our LLM business with respect to its ‘content supply chain,’” reads the Microsoft document, as quoted in the filing.

Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella also testified in a deposition earlier this year that “anything that is paywalled should be licensed by anyone who wants to use it…for grounding or training,” and made clear that, if he “had been made aware that OpenAI had scraped and trained on information that was behind a paywall,” he would have “invoked [Microsoft’s right to] require OpenAI to retrain its models.”

Other admissions cut against different pillars of the fair-use test: OpenAI’s head of ChatGPT, Nick Turley, wrote in internal communication that publishers face an “existential threat” from products like the chatbot, which are “largely substitutive” and “will get more and more substitutive as they get better.”

OpenAI President Greg Brockman described the models as “excellent at news.” Nadella agreed under oath earlier this year that conversing with chatbots “has substituted … giving you the information right there on the website on the AI platform versus needing to go to the underlying source.”

That kind of language speaks to how the technology could directly compete with, rather than transform, the original work.

A Microsoft document states that there is a “real risk” that generative AI could “significantly disrupt the employment of the very people who generated the data on which the foundation model was trained.”

The sheer scale of the copying is striking. The documents reveal for the first time that OpenAI’s mid-training datasets alone contain more than 91,692 copies of works published by the NYT, Daily News, and Center for Investigative Reporting. A Common Crawl-derived dataset included more than 2 million documents from nytimes.com alone.

In a January 2023 internal memo, Hecht called it “an astonishing theft of unprecedented proportions” and “the largest theft of labor in human history.”

The filing lays out in new detail how OpenAI and Microsoft went about acquiring the plaintiffs’ content, including scraping it from the Bing Index.

“OpenAI delivered the entire GPT-3 training dataset to Microsoft, which Microsoft used to evaluate how to implement OpenAI’s models within its own commercial products,” the filing reads. “Microsoft similarly provided training data to OpenAI through initiatives called Project Taxi and Project Mango.”

The companies allegedly assembled the Project Mango data into a training dataset that contains copies of at least 160,903 unique works from the news publishers.

In order to get the most out of their scraping, OpenAI employees allegedly came up with a plan to circumvent paywalls without detection. The filings show that when OpenAI researcher Nick Ryder told Brockman about a “hack to get around nytimes paywall,” Brockman replied: “ah nice.”

OpenAI employees also allegedly built training datasets like WebText and WebText2 that disproportionately relied on scraped news content. They also allegedly pulled millions of articles from Common Crawl, a free, open repository of web crawl data. The findings also describe deliberate efforts to strip copyright notices from training data before it reached the model, since researchers “wouldn’t want model outputting” “copyright notices” to users.

“The evidence revealed here for the first time shows that OpenAI and Microsoft knew that what they were doing was wrong,” Steven Lieberman, counsel for the New York Daily News, said in a statement shared with TechCrunch.

OpenAI and Microsoft did not return requests for comment.

title: Sutton's predictions v legendary guitarist Johnny Marr
description: BBC Sport football expert Chris Sutton takes on legendary guitarist and Man City fan Johnny Marr, plus the BBC readers and AI with his predictions for this weekend's Premier League fixtures.
fullText:
The pressure is growing on Manchester United boss Michael Carrick, but can his side sign off for the three-week international break by beating Fulham on Sunday?

"For teams who have had a bad start to the season, United being one of them, it could be a horrible few weeks," said BBC Sport football expert Chris Sutton.

"Any negativity is going to just fester, really. There will be speculation about his future, along with all the talk about whether this is a good time to replace your manager.

"United are not the only team to have made a bad start, but there is a lot to ponder on for them at the moment. It makes this weekend even more important."

Sutton is making predictions for all 380 Premier League games this season, against AI, BBC Sport readers and a variety of guests.

For week four, he takes on legendary guitarist and Manchester City fan, Johnny Marr.

Marr's new album, The Age Of Everything, is out on 2 October.

Do you agree with their scores? You can pick your own below.

The most popular scoreline selected for each game is used in the scoreboards and tables at the bottom of this page.

A correct result (picking a win, draw or defeat) is worth 10 points. The exact score earns 40 points.

Want to make more predictions? You can play BBC Sport's new Match of the Day predictor game every week, featuring six fixtures from domestic and European competitions.

Marr has enjoyed City's 100% start to the new Premier League season, with Sunday's win at Old Trafford continuing their impressive start under new boss Enzo Maresca.

"I think that derby will be remembered by City fans for a long time," Marr told BBC Sport.

"We all feared the worst when Phil Foden was sent off so early, because you don't know what could happen. It should have been a yellow card for him and Bruno Fernandes anyway.

"It's all a bit of a learning curve for the fans and the club with a new manager and so many new players, so to see how the team dug in and won was so great for City fans.

"No-one expected Maresca to win his first four games... but then again, why not? He's shown that he's his own man with his own philosophy. I like him."

Chris Sutton and Johnny Marr were speaking to BBC Sport's Chris Bevan.

The AI predictions were generated using Microsoft Copilot Chat - we simply asked the tool to 'predict this weekend's Premier League scores'.

Gtech Community Stadium, 20:00 BST

Chelsea are free-scoring and their front-line is so dynamic - but they are leaking goals left, right and centre and they are a bit of a rabble at the back.

I do think Chelsea will stop conceding eventually, but finding the right balance between defence and attack is Xabi Alonso's big problem at the moment because it is far too easy to create chances against his side.

Brentford boss Keith Andrews has got that balance in his team. They are very dangerous on the counter-attack, so you have to think they will hurt Chelsea too.

This fixture finished in a 2-2 draw in September last year, and I can see it going the same way this time.

Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, 12:30

Tottenham boss Roberto de Zerbi has this reputation of being a great coach, and we saw what a good job he did at Brighton.

But we have not seen any improvement from Spurs yet, despite the big money they have spent, and he is surely going to come under pressure soon if their poor results continue.

They are not the only ones to revamp their squad but if you listen to De Zerbi, after about five years they might come good.

He keeps saying they need time, but he has had long enough for their results to be much better already. Other clubs, like Hull and Ipswich, have brought plenty of players in and are doing well enough - so why aren't Spurs?

I think De Zerbi has to come under scrutiny, but it is different with Unai Emery at Aston Villa.

They are also without a league win, but they look more likely to score goals, as they showed against Coventry in the Carabao Cup on Wednesday.

I am expecting Villa to improve the same way they did after not winning any of their first five games last season, and I can see them edging this.

Do I give Spurs their first league goal of the season? Yes, but only one. They are due a deflection, or Villa will score an own goal.

Something will go for them, but not the result.

There might be a bit of an edge to this one after Brighton boss Fabian Hurzeler had a pop at Arsenal over their time-wasting when they beat the Seagulls near the end of last season.

I love the way Brighton play and I was at Old Trafford to watch their comeback to beat Manchester United in the Carabao Cup on Wednesday.

It doesn't seem to matter who they are missing from their team, Brighton are just bold as brass with the way they press and get men forward.

Luka Vuskovic, who they got from Spurs for £46m in the summer, is only 19 but he strolled through the game against United. What a player he looks.

The issue I have with Brighton in this game, however, is that Arsenal are not Manchester United. They are a cut above that.

Arsenal are the real deal and I don't see any weaknesses in their team, as their impressive win at Sunderland underlined. They are brave going forward, but they are also street-wise defensively and can see out a game when they have to, time-wasting or not.

They have that steel about them but I also think they could expose Brighton if Hurzeler's side go toe-to-toe with them, which is what I am expecting.

I nearly went for an Ipswich draw last week but changed my mind and went for Crystal Palace to win.

That meant I'd predicted Ipswich would lose their first four league games and they are joint-bottom of the table based on my predictions (see bottom of page).

Gary O'Neil's side have obviously done much better than that in reality - I know Palace went down to 10 men last week but, even so, well done to the Tractor Boys for finding a way to win that game.

Fair play to them, I like the ambition the club's owners have shown in the transfer market, and I really like the way O'Neil sets his team up. They are not just there to sit in in games, and they have got their reward.

I still fancy Everton to win this, though. They have made a great start to the season to stay unbeaten so far and, under David Moyes, they are a battle-hardened, resolute and well-organised outfit.

As a former Norwich striker I often get accused of being biased against Ipswich, but I am not being overly negative about them here.

I just see it being a tough afternoon for them, without getting a goal, and then a long trip home for Ipswich fans on the A14 - hopefully they don't close any of the major roads on Saturday so it is not an even more miserable journey back for them.

I can see this being a frustrating afternoon for Newcastle because they are going to come up against a Hull team who are brilliant at defending the box but are also brave with the way they throw people forward.

They are a threat from set-plays too but they have got the bit between their teeth and their whole attitude seems to be 'attack the Premier League' after getting promoted, which I really admire.

Along with Ipswich, Hull are the only other team I've predicted to lose all their games so far.

I am going to tip them not to lose this time... so you know what is probably going to happen. Apologies in advance to Tigers fans, because this happened with me and Sunderland last season.

Coventry were served up a couple of shockers by getting Arsenal and Manchester City as their first two away fixtures and this trip is far from easy for them either.

In fact this is another stinker of a game for Sky Blues boss Frank Lampard, because they are still struggling while Oliver Glasner seems to be getting Nottingham Forest going after a slow burner of a start.

There is a strong chance that Coventry's confidence has been sapped already so Lampard will be trying to rally the troops and give his players some belief that they can compete at this level.

That is going to be really difficult because they must be looking at the results of the other promoted teams and not just thinking 'where is a win coming from for us?' - but also 'where is a point coming from?', and 'where is a goal coming from?' too.

I don't think they will get any of those things this week, because Forest are looking pretty solid.

Well done to Forest striker Liam Delap by the way, who got his first goal for them in last week's win at Aston Villa.

He had a tough time at Chelsea, and I know what that is like, so it is great to see him off the mark for his new club.

My value went down by almost 50% when I left Stamford Bridge - from £10m to £6m - so what has gone on there?

Seriously, though, sometimes you need a change of scene to find your form again and Delap must be feeling a bit freer now he has his first Forest goal.

I am not convinced by Liverpool at all after covering them for Radio 5 Live last week - I thought Fulham were the better side in their 0-0 draw at Anfield.

Andoni Iraola's side did not flow in the final third, certainly not in the way his Bournemouth team did last season.

I don't think the Reds players are quite in sync with what Iraola is asking them to do in terms of their press either, and Fulham played through them with ease at times.

Marco Rose is an attacking manager so if Liverpool don't buck their ideas up then Bournemouth are going to do the same, and Iraola could end up losing on his return to his former club.

The one thing in Iraola's favour is that Bournemouth seem to be finding a way to draw games that they should win, so that is the result I am going with even though though I quite fancy the Cherries to take all three points.

I think I am in love with Leeds boss Daniel Farke. What a guy.

We were talking about him on the Monday Night Club before Leeds walloped Newcastle and only idiots question whether he is the right man to move the club forward now.

To see them beat Newcastle, and how emphatically they did it, was massive and more proof of their progress.

In contrast, Crystal Palace are almost on the precipice after their shaky start under new manager Pierre Sage, and I just don't see the Eagles getting anything here.

Leeds are so well organised at the back with new goalkeeper James Trafford, who is an upgrade on last season, and and a new centre-half I like too, in Tarik Muharemovic.

Apart from me, no-one else could say Muharemovic's name on the Monday Night Club, not even the posh Rory Smith, which I quite enjoyed.

Dominic Calvert-Lewin is flying up front, as well. He is fit, motivated and a real handful, which is another reason I can't see past a Leeds victory.

Sunderland are a really good team and, on their day, they are more than a match for anyone.

The Black Cats are strong and robust, and when they get after teams and press you then they are phenomenal.

All of that makes me think this is a really hard game for Manchester City.

Their derby victory was a brilliant win and Maresca's biggest result as their manager so far, with the way they did it.

Iliman Ndiaye showed what a good signing he is when he came on for Rayan Cherki in the second half at Old Trafford, in terms of offering a different profile.

Cherki's more of an inside forward, as a number 10 or playing narrow, and he's a guy where you think you couldn't get the ball off him in a telephone box.

Ndiaye, though, will do more work going back and is also more of a ball carrier, so he was exactly what City needed when they went a man down.

United can feel hard done by because City's winner should have been disallowed, but City were the better team with 10 men.

This will be a very different task for Maresca's men, with the emphasis on them breaking down the Black Cats, but I don't feel it will just be one-way traffic.

I still think City will find a way though, and they need to for the sake of the title race. They already seem to be the only team capable of keeping pace with Arsenal.

Johnny on former boss Pep Guardiola, who stepped down in the summer, and his favourite City players: No-one expected Pep to stay for 10 years so it made him leaving OK to accept, and good luck to him. Aside from the success he brought to the club, City fans loved him because he totally loved Manchester.

Dennis Tueart was my favourite player when I was a kid and I think he could have played in this current era. We've had amazing players in the last 12 or so years so how do you pick, but my favourites would be Vincent Kompany, Sergio Aguero and David Silva, with the top place going to Kevin De Bruyne. I'd say he's the best player I've seen in a City shirt.

Watching Fulham draw at Anfield last weekend changed my view on them.

I had not seen Alvaro Arbeloa's side over 90 minutes before and, while their other results were poor, this time they were excellent.

They cut through Liverpool and had some nice patterns of play, but also defended well too. Arbeloa said afterwards that they played with more balance and I think that is a good way to describe their display.

Then I went to Manchester United's defeat by Brighton in the Carabao Cup on Wednesday, and their performance was very poor.

Carrick really needs a response with a win here to take into the international break but how can I give United a chance, after the way the Seagulls absolutely dismantled them?

Three times in the past four seasons, United have gone to Craven Cottage and nicked the win late on, but I can't make a case for that happening.

As well as having problems up front, United are struggling defensively and I can see Fulham creating plenty of opportunities against them too.

Chris and his guest, Dorking Wanderers boss Marc White, both got four correct results with no exact scores from the 10 games in week four, giving them 40 points each.

AI did better, thanks to an exact score for Brentford's 2-2 draw with Bournemouth which, along with two other correct results, gave it a total of 60 points.

But it was the collective efforts of the BBC readers who took the weekly win - their first of the season - that also sees them move from bottom to level on points with Chris at the top of the predictions table.

They also got one exact score - Arsenal's 2-0 win at Sunderland - but also managed four correct results, giving them a total of 40 points.

It was a tough week for predictions, with only two games where everyone picked the right outcome - that victory for the Gunners, and Brighton's win at Coventry.

There were five games where none of our predictors guessed the result - Nottingham Forest's win at Aston Villa, Hull's draw at Chelsea, Ipswich's win at Crystal Palace, Fulham's draw at Liverpool and Leeds' win over Newcastle.

The biggest shock of the week came at Anfield. From more than 33,000 predictions, just under 30,000 (91%) of you went for a Liverpool win, while fewer than 2,000 of you went for any sort of draw and only 390 of you got the correct 0-0 scoreline.

fullText:
It’s a chaotic time in an industry that’s reshaping our lives – Guardian reporters and experts recommend the books that help explain how we got here, and where we’re heading

Have you been feeling trapped in an endless cycle of artificial intelligence hype and panic? You’re not alone.

It’s a chaotic time to make sense of the industry that’s reshaping our lives, whether or not we like it. Last week, another AI company employee publicly resigned, warning the technology “could kill us all by the end of the decade”. Despite these dire warnings, AI companies have seen “otherworldly” surges in revenue and driven the US stock markets to new highs as they continue to push AI tools into everything from public school classrooms to law enforcement agencies, as well as rushing to put up new datacenters across the country.

Thankfully, the Guardian’s tech reporters – and a few other tech experts we respect – are here to help. We’ve compiled an essential reading list of smart books that explain and critique the AI industry; books that, while flawed, illustrate key viewpoints in the AI debates; and a few books that provide deeper political and social context, including some works of speculative fiction.

The most intensively reported book on the AI industry so far, Empire of AI covers the rise of OpenAI, as well as the formation of Anthropic and OpenAI chief Sam Altman’s split with Elon Musk. Parts of the book can feel a bit inside baseball, but the reporting is great and shows how the key American AI companies brought us to this point. Some early reviews of the book in 2025 suggested Hao’s take on the industry was overly negative: she has since been entirely vindicated.

An in-depth look at how the US military and Palantir worked together to build autonomous weapons and surveillance systems that are an actual catastrophic threat – not an imagined one.

From the journalist and host of the Tech Won’t Save Us podcast, this is a deep investigation into the physical impact of AI data centers around the world, and the toll they are taking on local communities and the global environment.

Your Face Belongs to Us – Kashmir Hill

A bestselling book on the rise of Clearview AI, the facial recognition company that has provided sweeping surveillance powers to law enforcement, businesses and billionaires, by building a massive database of online images.

The AI Con – Emily M Bender and Alex Hanna

In response to claims that AI will soon far surpass all human capabilities, and that the technology is advancing so quickly it’s on the verge of becoming a new life form, the authors of The AI Con have a simple response: “LOL” and “they wish”. These two tech critic academics argue that this kind of rhetoric is “AI hype” – lies and exaggerations that are helping rich people make more money “by justifying data theft, motivating surveillance capitalism, and devaluing human creativity”.

If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies – Eliezer Yudkowsky and Nate Soares

If you want to understand the perspective of the people panicking that AI will destroy humanity, this book is a good place to start. It’s a “doomer classic” that has been described as a book-length version of the tweet that made everyone freak out this past week. Unfortunately for readers, its predictions of doom are based more on grand thought experiments than on an engagement with how AI is currently playing out in the world. The book “reads like a Scientology manual”, a New York Times reviewer wrote. For context, Yudkowsky’s other writings include a nearly 700,000-word work of Harry Potter fan fiction in which Harry applies the scientific method to magic.

Superintelligence – Nick Bostrom

This 2014 book is one of the foundational AI texts for people like Elon Musk, who, alongside Bill Gates, has publicly praised the bestseller. While the book is useful as a way of understanding the evolution of arguments about how a superintelligent AI might doom society, it’s worth noting that the author is a controversial Swedish-born philosopher who was forced to apologize in 2023 for a decades-old email in which he claimed “Blacks are more stupid than whites” and used the N-word. In 2024, Oxford quietly shut down the academic institute he had run, and Bostrom resigned.

Genesis: artificial intelligence, hope, and the human spirit – Henry Kissinger, Eric Schmidt, Craig Mundie and Eleanor Runde

Are you looking for AI insights from a man who faced frequent, wide-ranging and substantial allegations of war crimes? Astonishingly, Henry Kissinger, the former US secretary of state who died in 2023, co-authored a bestselling 2024 book on AI with a billionaire former Google CEO, a less-wealthy former Microsoft executive, and a young lawyer who worked as Kissinger’s researcher. The authors suggest that AI’s ability to provide swift answers without explaining how it got them might end our current “age of reason” and lead humanity back to a “pre-modern acceptance of unexplained authority”. They also raise the possibility that “the companies that own and develop AI will accrue totalizing social, economic, military and political power”, or that AI itself might become an all-powerful “philosopher king”. OpenAI’s ChatGPT listed this as one of the five best books on artificial intelligence.

The Technological Republic – Alex Karp and Nicholas Zamiska

This manifesto by the CEO of Palantir was described by one Guardian colleague as one of the worst-written books he had ever read. It includes rambling attacks on the Palestinian American academic Edward Said, and goes further than Kissinger and his co-authors by more or less calling for turning tech leaders into philosopher kings. Prose aside, the book provides an important window into what top tech CEOs actually believe, and the way they regard AI and tech as a new nuclear bomb – which, in their view, is a good thing.

The Rise and Fall of the Artificial State – Jill Lepore

A historical look at the political and industrial movements that have wanted to cede human agency and democratic rule to automation and authoritarianism. Just published, and a surprisingly fun read!

More Everything Forever – Adam Becker

Automating Inequality – Virginia Eubanks

This 2018 book predates the generative AI boom, but it provides an essential view into how automated systems and algorithms reinforce social inequality. Modern AI has supercharged these same capabilities and is getting integrated into every critical system, making the book’s insights into the harms of automated inequality even more important.

Predatory Data: Eugenics in Big Tech and Our Fight for an Independent Future – Anita Say Chan

Our current systems of techno-surveillance and algorithmic discrimination are rooted in 19th-century campaigns against immigration and in favor of eugenics, the practice of selectively breeding humans to improve their intelligence or racial dominance, Chan argues. The book highlights the evolution of “techno-eugenicists” and the persistence of feminist and immigrant activists who have fought against them, and is recommended by Seeta Peña Gangadharan, an associate professor at the London School of Economics who studies the community impact of data-driven technologies.

Prophecy: Prediction, Power and the Fight for the Future, from Ancient Oracles to AI – Carissa Véliz

Tracing the parallels between ancient seers, court astrologers, and contemporary algorithms, an Oxford University philosopher argues that “the main promise of prediction is not knowledge of the future but domination over others.” Another recommendation from Peña Gangadharan and her LSE doctoral student, Anna Osterberg, who studies the political dynamics of online communities.

Though it was first published in 1950, Asimov’s collection of short stories on the ethics of human-robot interactions remains influential, including his “Three Laws of Robotics”, starting with: “A robot may not injure a human being or, through inaction, allow a human being to come to harm.” As humor writer Alex Blechman has pointed out, classic science fiction books and films remain deeply influential in the tech world, even though many tech companies seem set on engineering precisely the kinds of dangerous outcomes that science fiction warned against.

The Lost Books of the Odyssey – Zachary Mason

In 2007, a computer scientist from Palo Alto published a collection of 46 retellings of passages from the Odyssey – a book that riffs on the way narratives get revised, fragmented, and reborn. Mason was actively imagining the prose AI might produce long before the technology was available. Asked for his recommendations on AI-related books, Robin Sloan, a fiction author and media and technology writer, chose this novel, which he called “the first book of the LLM era, even though it was written entirely, and beautifully, by a human”. He says the book “has a lot to say about multiplicity, deep stories and symbols”.

Sloan also made the case for a classic, Borges’ short story collection Labyrinths, as a book that “gets your head in the right place to think usefully and richly about the deep weirdness and enormity of language models”. The collection includes one of Borges’ most famous stories, The Library of Babel, first published in 1941, which describes and wrestles with a plan for an infinite library.

Nick Robins-Early contributed reporting

title: Could AI really end humanity? Post your questions for our tech reporters now
description:
After a week of alarming warnings about the technology’s potential to destroy the world as we know it, our expert tech reporters will take your questions on the reality of the AI threat. Join us at 3pm BST (4pm CEST, 10am EDT) where they will answer live
Sign up or sign in to ask your question

title: ‘Brutal’: thousands of T-shirt designs stolen and listed on Temu, Sydney label claims
description: Warwick Levy, who runs Lonely Kids Club, says AI may have been used to scrape his entire website and replicate...
fullText:
Warwick Levy, who runs Lonely Kids Club, says AI may have been used to scrape his entire website and replicate designs

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

After 15 years running a small business making T-shirts, Warwick Levy says it was “brutal” when he first discovered an identical design for sale on Temu.

It turned out there was an overwhelming amount of T-shirts identical to his own for sale on the Chinese e-commerce marketplace. Between 2025 and earlier this year, Levy, 37, found thousands of rip-offs.

“It’s pretty gut-wrenching to see that your work is now making so much money for other people that you don’t know, [who has] just stolen your work,” says Levy, who produces the graphic T-shirts at his Sydney label Lonely Kids Club in collaboration with local artists.

Levy urged Temu to take greater responsibility for copyright infringement by the merchants who sell products on its website, do more to stamp it out, and improve its complaints processes.

His story is the latest in a string of complaints by designers accusing major companies of facilitating theft of their designs, cases in which AI “scraping” tools may have been used to extract their art online before it was copied.

Despite original creative works being automatically protected by copyright law in Australia, making a claim of copyright infringement is not necessarily straightforward.

Amid broader concerns from artists and small brands about their designs being regurgitated by massive online retailers, the Albanese government is considering giving AI companies greater access to Australians’ content.

The government remains entangled in copyright negotiations with major AI companies, but the proposed reforms could give tech companies the legal right to scrape online content and use it to train their latest AI models.

Levy says he believed his T-shirts were copied by an AI tool which took the designs by scraping the entire Lonely Kids Club website.

“We have a catalogue of 4,000 products … all of those products were there with our exact item descriptions, our exact brand name, like everything, even our exact mock-ups that we’ve created and our own product photography that we’ve taken,” he says.

Levy, who notes that generative AI was not used in any of his T-shirt designs, says any government moves to facilitate the AI scraping of creative content would be “devastating”.

Ultimately, Levy says he was able to get Temu to take down the listings by making a trademark claim rather than a copyright claim over the designs, because the sellers were using the “Lonely Kids Club” brand name on their listings.

Levy says that attempting to complain to Temu was a stressful process full of “roadblocks”: the standard reporting forms kept failing or closing, and direct emails “got nowhere”.

He used his Australian trademark over his business name to bulk-report the listings and the overwhelming majority came down, although he said he had spotted some copycat T-shirts since then.

A Temu spokesperson said it was a marketplace used by independent sellers, whom it prohibited from listing products that “infringe intellectual property rights”.

“We have promptly removed the listings in question following Lonely Kids Club’s reports through our IP Protection Portal, and have added the brand’s works to our IP Protection database for ongoing monitoring,” they said.

“We take swift action to address any potential infringements once they are identified.

“Sellers are required to comply with applicable laws and platform policies, and those found to violate our IP policies are subject to enforcement actions, including listing removal, account suspensions, or permanent bans.”

Levy says Temu should hold itself and its sellers to a higher standard.

fullText:
Liberal MP speaks of AI’s shortcomings as cyber chief tells inquiry the tech is needed to fend off ‘highly capable malicious cyber actors’

Get our new political email, free app or daily news podcast

When a man with a terminal illness wrote to his local MP Andrew Hastie, telling him he planned on ending his own life with voluntary assisted dying, Microsoft Copilot suggested Hastie reply with “congratulations!”, “great to hear from you” or “that is wonderful news!”.

Hastie shared the episode at a parliamentary inquiry on Friday to underline the shortcomings of the American-run software as he called for AI run by Australians.

The hearing offered the some of the most detailed explanations of the Albanese government’s desire to bring Anthropic and OpenAI to Australia, in the face of calls to slow them down or shut them out.

The defence establishment told the inquiry that cutting the companies out could be catastrophic.

Abigail Bradshaw, the director general of the Australian Signals Directorate, said her agents needed advanced AI every day to fend off “highly capable malicious cyber actors”.

“If a digital adversary has access to newer, more capable models than we do, they may be able to identify and exploit vulnerabilities in systems and networks before we can identify them,” Bradshaw said.

But Australia’s top cyber-intelligence agency is “entirely reliant” on US-housed processing and would “dramatically” lose capability if cut off in a conflict, Bradshaw said.

The defence department’s chief AI officer, Chris Crozier, said the government was already trying to keep its tech needs local, contracting Google to build a series of interlinked datacentres spread across the country and disconnected from the US.

“Somebody can’t wake up and have a bad day and decide they’re going to turn it off,” Crozier said.

“We do not want to be using AI tool sets that are located offshore … we want the compute, we want the application, we want the data, we want the decision making, all based in Australia.”

Bringing big tech into the country would make the job much easier, he said, and not just by allowing the army to protect and maintain its datacentres.

The Office of AI, set up in the prime minister’s department, said bringing firms under Australian law would make it easier for local law enforcement to combat threats on the platforms.

Tight conditions on access could also materially improve Australia’s chances of using and defending itself with the best AI tools in the world, the inquiry heard.

“We will get more assured access, earlier access, more detailed technical access, and better integration with technical experts at the frontier,” Bradshaw said.

These would be assured by strict requirements on any top developers looking to train models in Australia, such as demanding government oversight and early access to advanced models, she suggested.

The government is already planning to set the rules for companies that come here. It is consulting on standards that would force AI companies to report issues and breaches and potentially reserve some computational power for local research.

Large datacentres will have to engage with communities, build away from schools and homes, and underwrite new renewables in most states.

Another pillar of the standards – copyright law – is yet to be settled, with AI developers refusing to train models here without law reform.

A proposal to give the companies access to everything Australians create online by default sparked a wave of backlash from creatives, who say the companies could pay for local licensing deals to access Australian content.

But Jenna Priestly, the assistant secretary at the attorney general’s department, on Friday confirmed looser copyright laws would also affect AI access to foreign-made content distributed in Australia.

She said the companies wanted to train models on “maybe billions” of pieces of information and claimed it was practically “impossible” to make deals with every rights holder.

“As Australia’s copyright framework protects not only copyright material that’s Australian in origin, but worldwide, I think it is a fairly large number that [companies] would need to go and strike deals with,” Priestly said.

The Greens senator David Shoebridge, who is among those fighting calls for copyright reform and demanding a pause on AI development, on Friday said Labor had refused him a seat on the inquiry committee.

Labor ministers have spent the week meeting with OpenAI’s vice-president, and Anthropic’s special envoy Jeff Bleich, who this week suggested Australia had just months to bring in effective regulation.

The attorney general’s department told Friday’s hearing the shape and timing of any copyright reform was yet to be decided. But the prime minister’s department said Anthony Albanese wanted draft laws on the broader AI standards by the end of 2026.

Australia’s chance for influence on and special access to the models could be at risk by a delay, Bradshaw said.

“Decisions around training are a matter of urgency,” she said. “I think it is inevitable that those providers will look at other places to locate.”

fullText:
Your AI reviewer flagged two instances of a bug. There are five. This fixes all five, runs your tests, and stops after three rounds.

A skill for Claude Code and Codex that clears AI reviewer feedback on your PR without you leaving the terminal. It reads real GitHub review-thread state, fixes what's actionable, sweeps the sibling instances the reviewer didn't flag, gates every push on your repo's own tests, and asks for re-review, hard-capped so it can't spam the PR.

Works with whatever AI reviewer assistance your repo already has. MIT, no server, no account, no vendor plan.

Claude Code — two slash commands:

Then, from a repo with an open PR that a reviewer bot has commented on (the loop asks which bot the first time, and remembers):

That's the whole interface. Other install paths · Prerequisites

Checkable claims, with the honest scope of each:

Reproduce the sweep. python3 evals/replay/replay.py runs two captured Sourcery reviews of PR #67 through the clustering and sweep code — no network, no arguments, stdlib only. The fixtures are that reviewer's real payloads, copied verbatim from the GitHub API rather than written for the demo. Run 1 merges two differently-worded findings into one pattern and reports 3 unflagged siblings; run 2 yields one site and correctly no sweep, because the same reviewer returned different findings on identical file contents.

If you're comparing alternatives, the closest is pbakaus/agent-reviews — broader bot coverage and a nicer CLI, no test gate, no hard round cap, no sibling sweep.

Note on Gemini Code Assist. Gemini is a first-class reviewer here and works exactly as it always did, automatic first review included, on the enterprise GitHub app. Google deprecated the consumer app 2026-06-18 and shut it down 2026-07-17, so it can no longer be installed on the free tier. Nothing about its support here changed. Select it with --reviewer gemini-code-assist.

--list-reviewers discovers which bots have commented on your PR; --reviewer persists your choice per PR.

Severity caveat, stated plainly: only two marker conventions are parsed today — Codex's ![P0]–![P3] and the ![critical]–![low] alt-text form Gemini uses. For any other bot every finding is unknown, so --min-severity high keeps everything and --drop-unknown-severity drops everything. Use severity filtering only with a bot whose format is parsed.

Bot reviewers expand. You fix the two instances of a pattern it flagged, push, and the next review flags three 

Three things in this loop attack that directly:

It sweeps the class, not the instance. Findings are clustered by a deterministic pattern signature. When one pattern is flagged at 2+ sites, sweep_siblings.py reduces those lines to tokens, intersects them, and reports every other line in the PR's changed files containing all of the shared tokens — the siblings the reviewer hasn't reached yet. A single multi-line finding can also fingerprint its normalized block and report exact copies as mirror candidates.

Intersecting across sites is the token sweep's safety property: a candidate has to match what the flagged sites have in common, not what any one of them happens to contain. Single-site mirror sweeps require a multi-line range and meaningful identifier-like tokens. The tool reports before anything is edited, refuses a single-line site or a too-generic shape, and never reads a file outside your diff. Swept patterns are tracked across cycles, so if one comes back you see ⚠ RECURRED after sweep instead of silently re-fixing it.

Mirror matching optimizes for precision over recall. By default, in every language, two blocks match only when their text is identical — no comment stripping, no whitespace collapsing, no per-language guessing. Comment-insensitive matching is enabled only for languages with a real tokenizer behind it, which today means Python alone, via the stdlib tokenize module (indentation is preserved, because it is semantic) — and only within a single file. Once comments are dropped, identical text can still mean different things in two different files: a .pyi stub versus a runtime module, one shebang or source encoding or from __future__ flag versus another. That list is the semantics of the whole toolchain and does not converge, so rather than enumerate it in the match key, normalized matching stays inside one file, where every such property is equal by construction. Those same files are still matched across files by raw matching, which claims only that the bytes repeat — a claim no shebang or encoding can falsify. So two .py files sharing a byte-identical block are still reported (as exact); two differing only in a comment are not. Python's raw index still carries the tokenizer's string tags, so it never matches a docstring's body against the code that docstring quotes. Blocks are never compared across language families, so identical text in build.sh and Makefile isn't called a duplicate. The trade is explicit: a duplicate in an unsupported language that differs only by a comment goes unreported. This is an advisory report — one that fires falsely stops being read, while a missed duplicate costs one informational finding.

It won't push red. Configure a verification profile once — a one-key menu pick on first run, auto-detected from your pyproject.toml / package.json / Cargo.toml / go.mod — and every cycle runs your own tests and linters before the commit goes up. A failed required check flips the run to verification: failed. Compare: CodeRabbit's autofix runs a build-verification step and ships the changes anyway when it fails.

It has a brake, not a timeout. The cycle cap is a hard count of re-review requests, default 3, and it counts only the agent's own pings — a human asking the bot to look again doesn't burn a cycle. That's a bound on rounds, not a "stop when the bot goes quiet for ten minutes" heuristic.

Everything else it does — reading isResolved/isOutdated off the reviewThreads GraphQL, honoring a maintainer's "wontfix" reply, sorting by severity, keeping one live-edited status comment instead of comment spam — is table stakes done carefully. Correct, but not why you'd pick this.

The -a flag selects target agents; omit it for the interactive picker. Requires a recent skills CLI. If codex doesn't appear in the picker, update the installer or use the Codex plugin flow above.

Omit the name to refresh every configured marketplace.

Settings, verification profiles, and run history are untouched on both — the first run after upgrading moves ~/.config/gh-gemini-review-loop/ to ~/.config/gh-review-loop/ and leaves a symlink at the old path for older installs.

Stuck on an old version? If your runtime insists you are already current while the releases page has moved on, the marketplace is pinned to a branch rather than tracking the default one. Both runtimes let you pin — Claude Code stores it as ref in ~/.claude/plugins/known_marketplaces.json; Codex stores it as ref under [marketplaces.<name>] in ~/.codex/config.toml, and accepts owner/repo@ref or --ref when adding. A pinned entry reports that branch's version as "latest" forever, and refreshing it changes nothing. Check with codex plugin marketplace list (Codex) or the config file above (Claude Code), then re-add the marketplace with the commands in this section to track the default branch again.

From a repo with an open GitHub PR:

See SKILL.md for the workflow definition, stop conditions, and every phrasing; the deeper material (sweep internals, judge eval, recovery, script reference) sits in references/ and is loaded only when a run needs it.

On the first cycle with actionable findings, the agent scans for build signals (pyproject.toml, package.json, Cargo.toml, go.mod) and offers a short preset menu: All detected · Tests only · Skip · Customize. Your pick persists under profiles["owner/repo"] in ~/.config/gh-review-loop/preferences.json; later runs are prompt-free.

Ask "Show review loop stats for this repo" (or run --stats). Metrics are local-only (~/.config/gh-review-loop/runs.jsonl), contain repo and PR number but no identity, and are never transmitted.

Per-run receipt. The full receipt is delivered to the PR, in the same live-edited comment the loop keeps there — status RUNNING per cycle, DONE or STOPPED at the end:

Your terminal gets one line pointing at it, so a long loop doesn't bury the conversation in repeated receipts:

A second model can label each finding (valid_actionable, false_positive, needs_human, explanation_only, duplicate, already_addressed) before you spend a cycle on it. Off by default; needs an OpenAI-compatible key. Calls go out over stdlib urllib — no SDK dependency.
